planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Abidjan holds its deepest near-black color best under strong indirect light and fades toward plain green in dim rooms.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix, watering when the top inch or two of soil has dried. Abidjan is a dark-leaved rubber tree sport whose broad, glossy leaves emerge with a reddish cast and mature to an intense purple-black that appears almost charcoal in lower light, distinguishing it from the more reddish-toned Burgundy cultivar. As a single-stemmed tree it develops an upright, architectural silhouette over time and can be pruned or air-layered to control height and encourage branching. Keep the plant away from cold drafts and heating vents, wipe the large leaves periodically to remove dust, and rotate the pot occasionally for even growth on all sides.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Belize needs more light than solid-green rubber trees to keep its pink and cream coloring from fading to green.

directions: Provide bright, indirect light and a well-drained potting mix, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. Belize is a patented tricolor sport of the rubber tree, its thick leaves splashed in shifting bands of deep green, gray-green, and creamy white, with new growth and leaf margins often flushed a distinctive rose-pink that is stronger and more consistent than in older variegated types like Tineke. Because the variegated tissue carries less chlorophyll, growth is slower and the plant is more prone to sunburn in direct sun and to reverting toward solid green if kept too dim, so bright filtered light is important for keeping the pattern vivid. Remove any shoots that revert to plain green as soon as they appear, and wipe the leaves occasionally to keep them clean and glossy.
sources: United States Patent and Trademark Office plant patent records

common_name: Schryveriana Rubber Tree (Vintage Gray-Variegated Rubber Plant)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; this older variegated cultivar is slower growing than solid-green rubber trees and colors best out of direct sun.

directions: Site in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix, watering once the top inch or so of soil has dried. Schryveriana is one of the older named rubber tree variegates, its leaves mottled in irregular patches of gray-green, dark green, and pale cream-yellow with an uneven, marbled edge rather than the crisp margins of more modern cultivars. Growth is noticeably slower than the species and the pale variegated tissue is more prone to leaf burn in strong direct sun, so consistent bright but filtered light gives the best color without scorching. Support the developing trunk as the plant gains height, clean the leaves periodically to keep them glossy, and protect from cold drafts and temperatures below 55 degrees Fahrenheit.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

common_name: Little Fiddle Fiddle-Leaf Fig (Compact Fiddle-Leaf Fig)

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Little Fiddle's compact, shrubby habit suits tighter indoor spaces where a full-size fiddle-leaf fig would quickly outgrow the room.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light indoors, allowing the top couple of inches of potting mix to dry between waterings. Little Fiddle is a dwarf, densely-branching selection of fiddle-leaf fig that produces the same glossy, deeply-veined, violin-shaped leaves as the species in a much smaller, bushier package, staying compact enough for a tabletop, shelf, or small-room floor spot without the aggressive upward growth of standard fiddle-leaf fig. Its naturally branching habit means it fills out sideways rather than racing toward the ceiling, and it tends to be somewhat more forgiving of average indoor light than full-size cultivars. Clean the leaves periodically to keep them glossy and photosynthesizing efficiently, avoid moving the plant frequently once it is settled, and keep it away from cold drafts and heating vents.

planting.note: Plant outdoors after all frost danger has passed in zones 10-12, or grow year-round as a houseplant in bright, indirect light; Nova's undulating leaflet margins give it a distinct texture among umbrella tree selections.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix or garden soil. Nova is a compact selection of the octopus tree distinguished by leaflets with pronounced wavy, undulating margins rather than the flat, smooth-edged leaflets of the standard species, giving the glossy compound foliage a ruffled, textured look while keeping a denser, less leggy growth habit than typical Schefflera actinophylla. It works well as a large container specimen on a shaded porch or patio in warm climates and can be brought indoors as a houseplant where winters are cold. Prune to control height and encourage branching, and keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since soggy conditions quickly lead to root problems.
sources: United States Patent and Trademark Office plant patent records

common_name: Geisha Girl Schefflera (Ruffled Dwarf Umbrella Tree)

planting.note: Plant outdoors after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May and bring containers indoors before temperatures drop below 35 degrees Fahrenheit in fall. Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage the dense, tight habit this cultivar is prized for.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix or garden soil. Geisha Girl is one of the most widely grown Schefflera arboricola cultivars, prized for its tightly clustered, cupped and slightly ruffled dark green leaflets that give the classic umbrella-shaped compound leaf a fuller, more textured look than the flatter-leaved species. Its naturally dense, compact branching habit makes it popular as a tabletop plant when young and as a substantial shrub or small tree as it matures, and it takes well to pruning and shaping. In zone 10-12 it can be grown outdoors year-round; in zone 9 treat it as a container plant moved indoors before cold weather arrives, and wipe the leaves occasionally to keep them clean and glossy.
